title: Accelerating fits in high-energy physics and beyond
abstract: Data analysis in particle physics often involves optimizing a loss function that quantifies how well a theoretical model describes the observed data, in order to estimate the parameters of the model. This is referred to as fitting. As datasets grow larger and more expensive analysis methods are used, the time required to perform this parameter estimation can be a limiting factor. This work explores techniques that can significantly accelerate the fitting process, and measures their performance on a set of example models chosen to be representative of a variety of physics fits. We compare the speed and precision of variants of several well-known optimization algorithms, namely Newton's method, BFGS, and the Migrad algorithm (commonly used in physics fits). We observe significant speedups when using some algorithms: most notably, some variants of BFGS are consistently about $10\times$ faster than Migrad across our benchmarks, while achieving the same precision. For quasi-Newtonian algorithms like BFGS and Migrad, we find that the initial value of the Hessian matrix has a large impact on the runtime. We additionally discuss methods for accelerating the evaluation of the loss function and its derivatives, using algebraic simplifications, automatic differentiation, and modern hardware features on the CPU and GPU. We find that basic algebraic simplifications of the loss function can significantly improve speed and precision. On the GPU we explore using mixed precision computation, and show that this achieves much higher throughput on most accelerators without significant precision loss. Lastly we discuss efficient parallelization strategies for both the CPU and the GPU. All of the techniques and algorithms in this paper are implemented in our new FastFit library, which was used for all of our benchmarks.

title: Activity-based temporal hypergraphs: from individual activity to collective social dynamics
abstract: Temporal hypergraphs provide an interesting representation for many social systems, as they integrate both the temporal and group nature of social interactions. Designing models of time-varying hyper-networks yields thus a convenient way to generate surrogates of empirical social systems, to understand the mechanisms underlying their emergent properties, and to investigate the evolution of dynamical processes taking place on such structures. Here, we focus on a specific and powerful class of these models, the activity-based temporal hypergraphs. We show how activity mechanisms provide control over the time scale of the dynamics, allow high modelling flexibility, and capture heterogeneity in agents' behavior. We also highlight how the activity can straightforwardly be extracted from empirical data to create surrogate datasets. We present paradigmatic examples of such models: the higher-order activity-driven models (HADx), which show that different underlying rules for the selection of active interactions produce different higher-order dynamics; the Emerging Activity Temporal Hypergraph model (EATH), able to generate surrogates of empirical systems by using higher-order mechanisms driven by both activity and group memory. We conclude discussing future perspectives for activity-based temporal hypergraphs, highlighting the potential of this framework to bridge realistic modelling of social dynamics with the study of the complex dynamical process they can support, from social contagion to opinion dynamics.
